"Nobody has ever had a crop off it," Marta said. "That is not the same thing as nothing will grow." She had been saying it to herself all week; out loud it sounded like somebody else's plan.

Fifty yards short of the piling the boat went soft on a sandbar and stopped. Oskar took the fare and shook his head at her look. "She will not float off with a load in her. It is shallow the whole way in."

Marta stepped out. Behind her the oarlocks started again, and she did not turn around to watch them go.
F3P14: Scientists once marked a small fish called a cleaner wrasse with a colored spot. After the fish saw itself in a mirror, it scraped its body against rocks. Some scientists said this proved the fish was self-aware, like apes and dolphins. We should be careful, though. Passing this mirror test may only show that an animal can link a reflection to its own body. That does not require any idea of a self. The wrasse's way of life gives a simpler answer. This fish gets its food by finding spots on other fish and picking them off. So it may be ready to react to a spot wherever it sees one, even in a mirror.
F3P15:
In 1849 the board of Hallowdean, a market town on the river Ledd, met to settle a six-year question: how to carry stone from the ridge quarries to the wharves. The board resolved upon a railway spur joining the town to the main line. Devitt's canal branch running down to the river wharves went down on the second reading.

Why the railway? Marrable told the board his furnaces would go elsewhere unless the work was begun, and the vote followed within a day. No covenant of repair binds Devitt or his heirs anywhere in the ledgers, which he kept himself. Thorne noted that the turnpike road carried across the high ridge was refused for want of a trust. The surveyors found the ground fit for every one of the four schemes. The quarrymen who petitioned for a horse tramway run down to the stone quarries went home empty. The roll of voting ratepayers was not enlarged in the eight years on either side of the vote.

Then came the check that Thorne recorded in his neat hand: a schedule of tolls so framed that the neighbouring carriers could not compete. No frost closed the work for a season, and the winter receipts never fall. The receipts of the first decade survive entire. The weighbridge returns were examined once a year at the audit, not weekly. Traffic rose steadily to the end of the decade. Numbered brass tokens belong to a later generation of gate practice, and none passed here.

One private source survives, the diary of Pell, the schoolmaster. Its worth is that it exposes an omission in the official record, the minute-book saying nothing of the members who withdrew. Pell was not present, and confirms no part of the account given in the official record. Foresight it did not show, the traffic never doubling as the members expected. The clerk entered the date twice, so the diary supplies none the official record leaves out. Circumstance did not force the choice so far that praise and blame are beside the point. Pell's memory has never been faulted, and his pages are no warning against trusting a private recollection. The board acted carelessly, and the praise later given it is not deserved. Narrow self-interest the papers will not bear out.
F3P16:
The mayfly hatch on Lake Ferrin once darkened the village streetlights for a week each June, and it has not done so since 2011. Five causes have been proposed: perch stocked for anglers, a dam trapping the silt the nymphs burrow in, fertilizer running off the lakeside farms, a raised weir drowning the shallows, and water warmer than before. Three summers of survey work point one way.

The surveys point to the dam. The silt the nymphs burrow in has not passed it since 2009, and the bed below is bare gravel. The stocked perch eat no nymphs, their stomachs holding snails. No algae bloom has formed; the farms' runoff stays low. The weir was never raised; its boards sit as in 1950. The lake runs no warmer than it did, June for June.

A spring feeds the north bay, a source of cold water all summer. Nothing climbs in that season; the shallows stay cold. The gauge holds no coil, working by float and chain. No trout leap for flies here, the lake having none. The trouble has no single origin anyone has found. The club's catch book dates the last big hatch to June of 2010. No change in the fishing appears there after the stocking. No members are named in it, only weights and dates. The catch book records no weather of any kind. No boast about the fishing is preserved there.

Return depends on passing silt below the dam, which a sluice could manage. Taking the perch out would gain nothing; the nymphs are safe from them. A buffer strip along the farms would catch runoff that never comes. Lowering the weir boards would uncover shallows never drowned. Cooler summers would help nothing, the lake being cool enough.

The club's conduct puzzles me; it paid for the survey and then ignored it. The club's conduct earns no praise from me. Its conduct rouses no anger in me. No hope comes to me from the club's conduct. Indifference is not what the club's conduct meets from me.
F3P17:
The grain hall at Ashbury was raised in 1729 and stood empty by 1848, its floor let out for hay. Five causes are named in the local histories: the mill's move upstream; the ending of the corn rent; the new canal to Marchford; the failure of the Ashbury bank; the fire of 1841. The parish records decide among them.

The mill did it. The mill went three miles upstream in 1836, and the carters followed it rather than turn back. Marchford's tolls never undercut Ashbury's, and the waggons kept coming. No fire touched the roof, whose trusses are the original oak. The corn rent ran on in kind until 1860, quite unchanged. The bank stood firm and trades today under the same name.

The charge of powder for the quarry was kept dry in the hall cellar. The porters took no fee, being paid by the vestry direct. Nobody was ever accused of anything within those walls. No bull ever rushed the market gate in living memory. The churchwarden had no duty there, the hall being the corporation's.

The churchwardens' book runs unbroken from 1701 to 1899. It supplies the carters: the new way past the upstream wheel is entered mile by mile. No tolls appear in it, Marchford's or Ashbury's. The August pages carry no fire and no loss of trusses. Payments in kind are absent from it altogether. No factor's dues are entered, and no page is ruled off.

Had the mill stayed at its old wheel, the hall would be trading yet; no other cause on that list emptied it, so no other rescue was possible. The credit here belongs to the churchwardens' book, and I give it gladly. The local histories are worth keeping, and I would throw none away. I offer the histories no correction on any single point. Nothing in them is comic, and the town believed them entirely. The vestry wrote down plenty, and I wish for nothing more.
F3P18:
For eleven days Ivo had been making a hare. It was to stand on the ridge of the Marchetti farmhouse: copper, hammered hollow, its ears set back as though it had just heard something move in the grass. On the twelfth morning he carried it up the stairs from the bench room, set it on Mrs. Hallam's table in the front shop, and put his hands behind his back so that she would not see them shaking.

She did not touch it at first. She walked around the table twice, the way she walked around a horse, and then she carried the hare to the window and held it up against the grey light of the yard. Petra, who had been four years with Mrs. Hallam and was allowed now to letter the invoices, went on ruling her lines and did not look up, which Ivo understood as a kindness.

"Here," she said at last, and turned the hare over so that the underside of the shoulder came into the light. The seam there was bright and a little beaded, run fast and hot in one pass. "You closed this in a single breath. It looks well this morning. It will look well next June. In the third winter the water will find the places where you did not wait for the metal to come up to you, and this shoulder will open like a seed pod."

Ivo asked whether he might carry it down again and open the seam and run it a second time, slowly, before it went anywhere. Mrs. Hallam said no. She wrapped the hare in sacking, wrote Marchetti, ridge, north face in the ledger, and stood it by the door for the carter, who came at ten. "It goes up as it is," she said. "The roof is a better teacher than I am, and it is slower, which is the whole of its advantage."

When she had gone out to the yard, Petra put down her pen. "She sent my first three up exactly as they were," she said. "Two came back inside four years. She knew which two, and she let the roofs tell me." Ivo went down to the bench room and opened the small book where he kept his measurements, and at the head of a clean page he wrote the day's date, and under it, Marchetti hare, shoulder seam; and then, lower down and in smaller letters, the date of the third winter from this one.
F3P19:
For three summers a crew from the Larkin Field Station camped at Muddy Fork Pond to explain one change in its golden shiners: the fish now spawn nearly three weeks earlier in spring than they once did. Records were thin: the cabin owners on the north shore photographed nothing, the hatchery that stocked the pond burned its paperwork, the graduate student of that decade left no notes, and the angling club never kept a logbook. The dates survive only in the field station's own automatic recorder, whose archive of the shallows through that decade still holds them.

The crew divided the shallow end into sixteen mesh pens and altered one condition in each group of four, leaving the rest of the pond untouched. Water reached the pens through an intake pipe, inside which a hard scale of lime had to be chipped out twice a summer.

A disease emptied the pond of bass a decade ago. Pens fenced against bass spawned eleven days ahead of pens the bass could enter, and their absence by itself moved the date. Pens warmed by a heater spawned on the ordinary schedule, so warmer water is not the trigger. Pens lit through cleared water spawned a little late, the opposite of what clarity predicts. Pens fed extra plankton spawned no earlier than untreated pens, which rules out an early bloom. Pens held at a steady depth kept the ordinary date, so the dam's release schedule explains nothing.

The crew expects the change to undo itself: bass are already working back up the inlet, and on their arrival the shiners should spawn late again. The crew will keep counting through the return of the bass, so the work at the pond is not finished. No second measurement is pending; the pens settled the cause, and the crew says so plainly. The crew had published nothing about the pond before, so no claim of its own is being withdrawn, and the same should be true of any pond that has lost its bass.
F4P1:
For centuries, the Dutch protected their low, flat country from rivers in the same way: by building dikes, long walls of earth that hold water back. When a flood broke through, people built the dikes higher. Each time, the taller walls seemed to solve the problem.

In 1995, that confidence was shaken. Heavy rain sent the Rhine and Meuse rivers surging, and about 250,000 people were told to leave their homes. The dikes held, but only barely. Engineers realized that raising the dikes had trapped the rivers in narrow channels. With nowhere to spread out, the water rose faster and pushed harder against the walls.

So the government tried a different idea, called Room for the River. Instead of fighting the water, engineers gave it space. In some places they moved dikes farther back from the riverbank. In others they dug side channels or lowered fields so that floodwater could spread out safely. A few farms were moved to higher ground.

The old dikes still stand along most rivers. But now, when the water rises, it has places to go.
F4P2:
A millstone does not grind by crushing. Its working face carries shallow grooves, called furrows, that scissor past one another as the upper stone turns, so that the grain is cut rather than mashed. Furrows wear flat within a few weeks of steady work, and a flat stone heats the flour and spoils it. Every mill therefore kept a dresser, or hired one who walked a circuit of the valley: a tradesman who lifted the runner stone, laid it face upward on trestles, and recut the whole pattern by hand with a steel pick.

He worked by eye. He set a lamp low at the rim so that every ridge threw a shadow across the face, and a furrow cut too deep swallowed its shadow instead of casting one. An apprentice spent his first year carrying lamps round stones he was not permitted to cut, until he could read a face at a glance.

The trade had its own vocabulary. A miller spoke of the charge of a stone, meaning the grain let down onto it from the hopper above, and no one outside the valley mills would have known what was meant.

Thomas Ede dressed stones in the valley mills for forty-one years. The French quarries that had supplied the valley's best stone closed during the war of 1870, and rather than wait for them, the owners bought iron plant in 1878 on credit. The old stones went into garden walls. Ede cut his last in 1883. The quarries were working again within four years, by which time no mill here could have used them; the trade ended less by a better method than by four years of impatience, and that is worth setting down plainly.
F4P3: Many people see farming as an obvious upgrade. Farming made more food, so foragers gladly took it up. Ancient bones tell a different story. Early farmers were shorter than the foragers who came before them. They also had more tooth decay and more signs of poor nutrition. Farming did produce more calories per acre. But those calories came from a few starchy crops, and they cost longer hours of work. Crowded villages also spread disease. So why farm at all? Perhaps once populations had grown, foraging could no longer feed everyone. Farming may have been less a prize than a trap: good for the group's numbers, but bad for each person's health.
F4P4:
Grieve's Salt Line was made in 1961, dropped after two seasons, and revived this month by the Vellacott company in a better version. Five changes are credited with the improvement: the casting of older dancers; the slower tempo of the score; the cutting of the third section; the restored side-lighting; the move to a smaller house. One of them does the work.

It is the tempo. Taken a third slower, the crossing steps land on the breath, and the dancers stop fighting the music. The lighting comes from overhead as before, and no shadow falls. The company is young, and the hesitations still read as error. The third section survives entire, argument and all. The house seats two thousand, and every gesture must be enlarged.

The score was recopied from the 1961 parts, and two errors in it corrected. Twenty dancers were never seen at any audition here. The boards are unmarked, and no scratch shows where the set stood. Nothing is unsettled between the company and the estate. No usher tallies the empty seats, ruled book or otherwise.

Grieve's programme note of 1961 is reprinted in the new booklet. The note leaves the tempo to the conductor, which is why the company may take it as slow as it likes. Lighting is fixed there too, the house given no say. It wants dancers of sixty, grey heads at that. The third section it calls the heart of the piece. The smallest room is what it asks for.

Restore the old tempo and the evening collapses; nothing else on that list is holding it up, so nothing else would save it. I have nothing to qualify: go, and take somebody who dislikes dance. Those dancers could give it nightly for a year; I wonder nothing. I have always liked the piece, and my liking was never questioned. The piece was never in danger of being lost; no rescue was needed. The applause is no louder than the evening warrants, and fashion explains nothing.
F4P5: (1) Lucia's class planted twenty bean seeds in paper cups. (2) Half of the cups sat on a sunny windowsill, and half sat in a dark closet. (3) After a week, the closet plants were taller, but their leaves were pale and their stems drooped. (4) ___ the class decided that height alone was not a good way to judge a plant's health.
F4P6:
We had been three days at my grandmother's house on Cardigan Street, and by Sunday afternoon there was almost nothing left to argue over. Nell had gone into the care home in March without ceremony, the way she did everything. My mother, Beatriz, had labelled the last of the crockery and was resting on the bottom stair when I prised the tin box out from under it. Nell had marked every other box in the house in her square capitals. This one carried nothing at all.

Inside were drawings, forty or so, on the soft grey paper of the seventies: horses, a bus, a woman with enormous hands. Every one was signed BEATRIZ in a child's block letters, and every one was annotated on the back in Nell's hand with a date and a remark. Hands still wrong. Better, but hurried. The albums she brought out for visitors had all been labelled; she had labelled everything she expected another person to open.

My mother turned three of them over and then stopped turning them. She sat down on the bottom stair with the horse in her lap and said nothing for a while. Then she said that she had been told at nine that she had no particular gift, and that she had believed it, and that she would rather I put the rest back in the tin.

I decided on the drive back that I had learned something cruel about my grandmother: that she had kept a scorecard on a nine-year-old, dated and filed, and had let the child read the verdict off her face for years afterwards. Forty drawings. Forty corrections. It seemed to me a very tidy way to make a person stop.

On Tuesday I sat with Nell by the window and showed her the woman with the enormous hands. She turned it over and read her own writing aloud, unhurried. "I was copying them," she said. "Thursday nights, after she had gone up. Hands still wrong meant mine." My mother had stayed down in the car park and did not come up, and I sat there holding forty years of the wrong story. I left the drawing on her table.
F4P7:
Every March the pale salamanders of the Radna hills leave the limestone crevices where they have wintered and travel, some of them two hundred meters, to breed in shallow rock pools. For most of the last century the standard account held that each animal remembered its route. Teodora Vasnev, a field biologist who had spent eleven winters in the hills, thought the account did no work. Memory, she liked to say, was the name of the puzzle and not its solution.

In 1996 she built something that let her ask a narrower question. Four artificial pools, identical basins of poured concrete, were sunk into a level clearing forty meters from any natural water, at the corners of a square eight meters on a side. She labeled them A through D. Under pools A and B she set a small motor that tapped the basin twice a second, the rate of water dripping from stone; under pools C and D she set motors that never ran. Nothing else about the four differed: the same water, the same depth, the same rim of gravel. At dusk she carried ninety-six adults from three home crevices to the center of the square and left them there.

Averaged over eleven nights across two springs, sixty-one of the ninety-six were in A or B by dawn, twenty-two were still in the open, and thirteen were in C or D. The pattern held on nine nights of the eleven.

The untreated pools were the informative ones. Pool D took no animal at all until, on the last three nights, she shifted it three meters east toward the release point; it then took thirty a night, more than either tapping pool. Vasnev put this in the body of the paper rather than in a footnote.

In the second season she drew the path of every animal on a sheet of waxed paper laid over a map of the clearing, to learn whether the animals approached the pools directly or by searching. The lines ran straight from the release point and bent only in the last two meters.

She published in 1999, in a journal few outside the region read, and for a decade the work was cited mainly by people who studied cave fish. What makes it worth reading now is less the cue she found than the way she isolated it: she built a clearing in which only one question could be asked at a time, and then reported the one result that spoiled the answer.
F4P8:
Over ten years, visits to every public library branch in this city fell — every branch but one. On the east side one small branch held its count steady, and in some years raised it. A team of researchers spent two years finding out why. The answer turned out to be a machine in the corner. The east branch alone stays open into the evening, yet in the month a failed boiler shut it at five with the rest, its daily count did not move. Children whose parents work late do gather there, yet the count stayed as high through the summer holiday, when the schools were shut and those children were at home all day. A rerouted bus line does stop at the branch door, yet when roadworks sent that bus three streets away for a month the count held firm. The same few people have worked that desk for years, yet the busiest month in the record fell while strangers stood at the desk.

The team set the branch against one across the river that had charged for printing after years of giving it away. That branch's count dropped the season the charge began, while here, where the printer queue ran longer than the desk queue, the count held level. The fortnight the printer here stood broken took a third off the daily count, the sharpest fall in the whole record.

After two years the team put the difference down to the printer, a machine nobody had thought worth counting. The branch had been marked for closing in a plan quietly dropped the week the election returns were counted, and nobody had asked why its count held. They admit plainly to surprise that the cheapest of the five explanations was the one left standing at the end. They will not say the finding would hold in another city; they do not fence the result inside this city either; they see nothing fragile in the arrangement; and they make no complaint against the officials who acted on other advice.
F4P9: Many people say that children who speak two languages are better at focusing. They are also said to switch between tasks more easily. The idea is that juggling two languages trains the brain. Early studies seemed to agree. But one scientist doubts it. She points out that many of those studies were small. She also notes that a study was more likely to be published when it found an advantage. She thinks this publishing pattern made the advantage look bigger than it really is. If she is right, she says, the research should show a telltale pattern.
F4P10:
Miss Arden taught ninth-grade composition in a room whose radiator knocked all winter, and she never apologized for the noise. She was not warm. She did not learn our names until October, and when she used mine it landed like a fact, not a greeting. What she had instead was exactness: she would stop mid-sentence, look at the ceiling, and begin the sentence again with one word changed.

In March she told us to keep a notebook — not a journal, she was firm about that, but a record of sentences we could not account for. I filled mine with the talk of the men at my father's garage, and one long entry, four pages, about the way my grandmother said goodbye on the telephone. I knew it was the only good thing I had made.

She gave the notebook back on Monday with nothing written in it — no check, no line, no comment, only a paperclip holding open the page about the telephone. I turned every leaf twice looking for ink. For three weeks I decided she had found nothing there worth the trouble of a pencil, and I stopped writing in the notebook altogether; the blankness felt like a verdict too polite to argue with.

I did not ask her about it for a long time. When I finally did, she was erasing the board and did not turn around.

"I mark what a writer can still repair by Friday," she said. "That page cannot be repaired by Friday. It needs a year and a colder eye, and a pencil of mine on it now would only teach you to want my pencil." Then she asked whether I had kept writing, and I lied and said yes.

Nineteen years later the school dedicated a new library, and I went out of a vanity I would not have admitted to. Miss Arden had died the previous spring. Her sister Nell was handing out programs by the door, and when I told her whose class I had been in she steered me to the window.

Miss Arden had copied my telephone page into a notebook of her own, Nell said, and kept it in a folder she labelled Not Yet — student pages she had refused to mark, reread every summer for thirty years. Standing at that window I understood that the blank margins had not been a verdict but a form of waiting, and that I had spent three weeks reading attention as indifference because indifference was the easier thing to believe. I have been wrong about silence often since.

Tolland Staithe stands at the end of a mile of causeway, and while the villages either side have emptied, its people stay. Five things are said to hold it there: the cheap cottages; the eel fishery; the summer ferry to Harnsey; the school that never closed; the causeway raised in 1978. The people who live there name one.

They name the ferry. The Harnsey boat runs from May to September, and the trade it brings pays for the winter. The causeway was never raised and floods forty times yearly. No eel has come out of the creek since the weirs rotted. The school shut in 1981, and the children go to Harnsey. Cottages here cost more than Harnsey's, and no incomer buys.

By nine the village is fast asleep, and only the marsh stays awake. The flood tide is slow here, and the flats take hours. The boats are moored to nothing and drift about the creek. The chapel gives up no meals; March passes like any month. The church clock keeps true time to the minute.

A tide table is nailed to the ferry shed door. It gives the boat: the sailings to Harnsey are ringed in ink from May onward. The flooded hours are left off it, being too many to ring. No ebb hour is ringed for nets; the eel men ignore it. The school bells are nowhere on it, and no crossings are timed. The spring tides are unringed, and newcomers get no warning.

Let the summer ferry stop and the Staithe empties like the rest; nothing else on that list holds it, so nothing else would keep it. I left on the Monday boat and have wanted to go back since. I would put no money on the Staithe lasting fifty years. The Staithe has weathered worse decades, and this one frightens me not at all. Visitors may call it unspoilt; the word does not trouble me. The Staithe complains of nothing, and I have no impatience.

My aunt Vesna keeps the accordion shop on Vrbnik Street, the one my grandfather opened with a borrowed lathe and a hand-painted sign he made twice, because the first one leaned. I spent July at the low bench under the window, holding parts while she named them. On the bench between us lay the instrument she had promised for the end of the month. It belonged to a nine-year-old on Petrinja Street whose mother had traded a winter of piecework for it. The girl would learn on it, badly, for years. Her teacher had asked only that the buttons be easy under a small hand, and that nothing on it be worth crying over.

"We build it forgiving, this one," Vesna said. "She will drop it. She will leave it beside a radiator. Everything we do has to survive a child who does not love it yet." So she fitted the straps a size short so that they could be let out later, and she left the dent in the grille where it had always been, because a scratch on a scratched thing costs a child nothing.

The instrument lay open the way something lies open on a surgeon's table: bellows folded back, reed blocks lifted out and stood in rows on a square of felt. Vesna worked without hurrying. She kept a chalk line down the middle of the bench, and everything she had touched went to her side of it. I found a reed that buzzed and swapped it for the sweetest one in the tin box of salvaged reeds on the shelf. Vesna lifted my reed out again, fitted a plainer one, and screwed the block down. "A beginner has to hear her own mistakes," she said. "Give her honey and she will never learn to listen." Then she packed the case in a canvas bag with a spare strap in the pocket. When the girl came for it she played four notes, every one of them wrong, and Vesna smiled as though the month had ended exactly on time.

Halvard Renn painted Low Water on an oak panel in 1908. By the time the Marchmont Institute acquired it, a patch of paint the size of a hand had gone from it. Four explanations lay before Nadia Brill, the Institute's conservator, when she opened the file. She ruled out the wax Renn stirred into his colors, which no test found in the panel; she ruled out the flood that reached the basement store, since the panel's back showed no swelling; and she ruled out the heat of the gallery lamps, which were installed long after the loss appeared. What remained was the varnish an earlier restorer had brushed on, a synthetic coat that shrank with age and pulled the paint up with it.

A photograph of the panel taken in 1931 is pinned inside that file. Brill reproduces it not to argue that the evidence for rebuilding is too poor to use, and not to furnish a pattern for rebuilding the lost passage, and not to show that the loss has spread since the print was made; she reproduces it to fix the date of the damage. In the print the bared wood is new, and its edges are still sharp.

The third section of her report is titled simply “The Ground.” The ground of the picture — the wet shingle Renn painted across the lower third — is where the loss falls, and its flatness eased the choice. Brill filled the gap with a flat neutral tone that matches nothing else. She did not leave the break open, as several of her colleagues urged; she did not rebuild the missing passage from Renn's surviving study; and she did not lay a removable glaze across the gap. A visitor today sees a plain block of color where the paint used to be.

My own view is approval, but not the wholehearted kind. I do not disagree with her reasoning, and I will not pretend to withhold judgment; I regret only what the choice cost. A neutral patch is honest about being a patch, and it also halts the eye at the one place Renn meant it to travel on, which is a price the picture will go on paying.

Priya had watched a dozen baking videos before her first Saturday at Aunt Lata's bakery, so when her aunt offered to show her how to knead the dough, Priya just shook her head. "I've got it," she said, and Aunt Lata only shrugged and went back to the ovens.

Priya's first loaf came out of the oven as flat as a plate, so she tried again, pushing the dough harder and longer, and the second loaf was even flatter. By noon her arms ached from all the pushing, and the trash bin by the door held three gray disks.

Aunt Lata never said a word about them, and she simply kept working at the long table, her hands folding and turning the dough.

At last Priya put down her bowl and walked over to the table. "Can you show me what I'm doing wrong?"

Her aunt pressed Priya's palms into the dough. "It's still sticky. Add flour a little at a time until it feels soft and smooth, like your earlobe."

"How much flour is that, exactly?" Priya asked.

"It depends on the day," Aunt Lata said. "Rainy days need a little more."

That afternoon, Priya's loaf rose tall and golden. She carried it to the front counter herself, but she kept glancing back to watch her aunt's hands.
F4P15: In the famous "marshmallow test," young children could eat one treat now or wait for two treats later. Those who waited did better later in life. Many took this as proof that self-control is a fixed trait. Some researchers now question that lesson. Waiting only makes sense if a promise can be trusted. A child who has learned that adults often break promises is being sensible by taking the sure treat. When experimenters first showed they were reliable, children waited much longer. When they proved unreliable, even "patient" children grabbed the treat at once. The test may measure not willpower but whether a child expects promises to be kept. That depends on how stable the child's home has been.

Kellerman's yard closes for good on the first of September, and I spent the last week of August there with my uncle Teodor. The launch Marisol stood on blocks in the shed, out of the water for the first time in forty years. My grandfather built her; Teodor ran her to the island and back for half his life. By Monday every house on the lake had a use to propose for her; by Friday she had a new owner. The marina at Two Harbours sent a cheque, and on Friday he signed it over to the bank. The sailing club had asked in June to teach beginners in her; he said a gift clears no debt, and no beginner boarded her. He had pushed a knife into her garboard plank in June; it went in no quarter inch, and no rot showed along her keel. The islanders would take the county's new boat; the crossing, he said, was no longer his. Petrus rowed over to trade his skiff and outboard; Teodor, who could still slip her single-handed, said a swap brings no money through the gate.

The bank had carried the mortgage since the bad winter, and the sum owed had grown past what a season of repairs could earn. Every other use proposed that week ended at the same wall: pay in September, or the doors would not open again. “The yard outlasts any boat in it,” he said, “and I will not shut these doors to keep one hull in the family.”

The sale drew half the lake to the shed on Friday, and I carried chairs out for people I had never met. He never asked the registry to put her name back on the list. I was not relieved, I was not proud of him, and nothing in it struck me as funny. There would be no crossing to dread in January; I was angry with him all evening, and knew even then the anger was unfair, since the cheque was the yard's one chance.

Havermouth, Maine, had shipped fish for eighty years before it had any way to keep them. The schooners came in on the tide, and whatever the crews could not sell on the wharf by evening went into salt or went to the gulls. In April 1911 the town raised the money, bought a compressor from a firm in Portland, and opened an ice plant at the head of the pier. By midsummer the plant was making twelve tons of ice a day, and Havermouth's fish began to travel.

The change the ice made was in the length of a trip. Before the plant, a schooner had to turn for home on the second day, whatever the fishing. With ice in her hold she could stay out nine days, and the average catch landed at Havermouth rose from eleven barrels a trip to thirty-four.

The cost fell first on the barrel yard. Salt fish had needed tight casks, and Havermouth had kept nine coopers and their apprentices busy the year round. Iced fish went out in cheap slat crates milled up the river. Within four years the plant drew the yard's last apprentices into its engine house, and the cooper's trade was gone from the town.

The town's records, kept through the plant's tenth year, show what the trade came to. In 1921 the six men who owned schooners reported incomes four times what they had earned in 1910. Wages for hired crew stood where they had stood, at eighteen dollars a month and a share. The plant had made the port richer without making most of its people richer, and the town meeting of that year argued about little else.

The compressor ran until 1946, when a larger plant at Beal's Point replaced it. By then no one in Havermouth could remember shipping fish any other way.
F4P18: When photos showed narrow gullies on the walls of craters on Mars, many people thought flowing water had carved them. If so, Mars might once have been friendly to life. The gullies do look like channels that water cuts on Earth. But looking alike does not prove the same cause. Many of the gullies sit in places too cold for liquid water to last. They are also most active in the middle of winter, not in summer. That is when frozen carbon dioxide, called dry ice, builds up and then turns straight into gas. So many scientists now think the gullies were carved by blocks of dry ice sliding on the gas they give off.
F4P19: Many people believe that time together makes rival groups less prejudiced. Decades of studies show that contact often does reduce bias. But the idea is not that simple. Early researchers said contact helps only under certain conditions. The groups must meet as equals. They must work toward shared goals, with support from leaders. Without these, contact can make hostility worse. Later studies also found that some of the benefit fades once people leave the planned setting. So the evidence supports a narrower claim. Carefully planned contact reduces prejudice. Simply being around another group will not do the job by itself.
F4P20: Most histories say Japan built factories quickly after 1868 for one reason. Its new Meiji government brought in Western machines and foreign advisers. The machines mattered, but they do not explain why Japan could put them to use when many other countries could not. Long before 1868, Japan already had high literacy, busy trade networks, and skilled village workshops. Its merchant houses kept careful account books. So the new machines met workers and managers who were ready to run them. Foreign experts were sent home as soon as Japanese workers could replace them, often within ten years. Japan's success came less from borrowing than from business skills it already had.

On the gravel flats of the Karoo, the mottled nightjar builds nothing at all. The female scrapes a shallow hollow in the open ground, lays two eggs the colour of lichen, and settles over them so still that a hiker can pass within a metre and never look down. The arrangement works: in four seasons of watching, fewer than one nest in ten was found by a fox or a crow. Which is what makes the birds' other habit so hard to explain. In roughly a third of nests the pair simply walks away. The eggs are intact; the two birds scrape a fresh hollow somewhere else and begin again.

Mira Osei spent those four seasons near Loxton, on her knees with a notebook, counting hollows. The departures were not scattered evenly. They tracked the temperature of the ground: days when the flats passed fifty degrees at midday were followed, four times in five, by an abandonment, while a cool week produced almost none. The pattern held in early nests and late ones alike.

The obvious suspect was predation — a fox passing close enough to unsettle a pair without ever finding the clutch. Osei tested the idea by moving eggs between hollows. Eggs carried to a hollow in the morning shade of the dolerite ridge were sat through the hottest week of December, whatever pair had laid them. The same eggs' parents, left out on the open flats, walked off within three days. The trigger travelled with the ground's heat, not with the clutch or with the birds.

The pairs that left did not stay low; the new hollow lay on average nine hundred metres uphill, on the dolerite ridge where rock holds the morning cool. Osei read ground temperatures at both. The open flats reached fifty-four degrees by one o'clock; the ridge hollows stayed near thirty. By January the heat had put a check on laying everywhere below the rock, and every hollow still occupied lay above it.

None of this makes the nightjar a planner. The bird holds no model of the season in its head; it holds a rule, and the rule was shaped by what the flats did to birds that lacked it. What the case offers is a reminder that behaviour which looks like waste from the outside may be the cheapest line in the animal's budget — and that the way to find out is to count, for four seasons, the things nobody thought worth counting.
